newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin's defence chiefs agree - future looks black.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin's defence chiefs agree - future looks black.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's two military chiefs put aside differences on army reform on Friday and combined to paint an apocalyptic picture of Russia's armed forces if military changes are further stalled.

"The armed forces have approached a critical stage," Yuri Baturin, secretary of Yeltsin's consultative Defence Council, told a joint news conference with Defence Minister Igor Rodionov. Both men cast doubt on the feasibility of a switch ordered by Yeltsin to a professional army.
"If things go on like this for another two years we may have a Navy without ships, an airforce without planes and a military industry incapable of producing modern weapons," he said.

Interfax quoted Rodionov as saying on Thursday that Russia was on the verge of losing control of the nuclear forces that established the Soviet Union as a military superpower and remain a major diplomatic bargaining chip for Russia.

"No one today can guarantee the reliability of our control systems," he told invited Russian journalists. "Russia might soon reach the threshhold beyond which its rockets and nuclear systems cannot be controlled." For lack of money he was being reduced to a spectator of the armed forces' decline.
On Friday the minister who has been known to use apocalyptic predictions to elicit money for the army, appeared to tone down his remarks.
"So far all systems are under control and even foreign intelligence reports praise the state of affairs in the strategic nuclear forces," he said.

Yeltsin, who is convalescing in his residence outside Moscow after double pneumonia, ordered Baturin and Rodionov to appear in public to dispel widespread and persistent media reports of a bitter rivalry over who is to spearhead reform.
"Rumours about what they describe as our rivalry are unfounded," the 60-year-old former general said.
"We may express different views. But it is the commander-in- chief (Yeltsin) who issues final orders which we have to obey."

The armed forces debate has taken on a keener edge with the approach of a NATO eastward expansion. Russian officials are contemplating steps to guarantee national security but Moscow's bargaining position is weak while the forces are in disarray.
The two defence chiefs contrast by character and background.
Rodionov is a career officer, far more closely wedded to the interests of servicemen than the lawyer-turned-politician Baturin.

According to Russian media reports, Rodionov is pressing for considerable extra funds to finance reform. At the same time the forces face an immediate crisis over soldiers' unpaid wages, miserable conditions, corruption and plummeting morale.
"The key question is not holding conceptual debates but rather solving a problem of where to get the money for the reform," Baturin said.

Rodionov said his ministry currently controlled a force of 1.7 million servicemen. Baturin added that together with forces reporting to other ministries Russia had about 2.4 million people in military and para-military service.
Rodionov complained that the draft 1997 budget allocated for defence spending 50 trillion roubles ($8.9 billion) less than what he called the minimum needs of the struggling armed forces.
He said that with this money he could only save the armed forces from final decline, nothing else.
"Our task now is to preserve personnel, technical structures, training systems in anticipation of the time when our economy will allow us to spend enough money on proper military reform."
Both officials appeared sceptical about a Yeltsin decree ordering an abandonment of traditional conscription and introducing a fully professional army by 2000.
"I think it is unreasonable and impossible for Russia to switch to fully professional armed forces," Baturin said.
"We can only dream of a professional army at this stage," echoed Rodionov.
